0.content: A View to a Kill is a 1985 spy film, the fourteenth in the James Bond series produced by Eon Productions, and the seventh and final appearance of Roger Moore as the fictional MI6 agent James Bond.

1.document_name: Wikipedia: A View to a Kill
1.content: Although the title is adapted from Ian Fleming's 1960 short story "From a View to a Kill", the film has an original screenplay.

2.document_name: Wikipedia: A View to a Kill
2.content: In A View to a Kill, Bond is pitted against Max Zorin (played by Christopher Walken), who plans to destroy California's Silicon Valley.

3.document_name: Wikipedia: A View to a Kill
3.content: The film was produced by Albert R.

5.content: Wilson, who also wrote the screenplay with Richard Maibaum.

6.document_name: Wikipedia: A View to a Kill
6.content: It was the third James Bond film to be directed by John Glen, and the last to feature Lois Maxwell as Miss Moneypenny.

7.document_name: Wikipedia: A View to a Kill
7.content: Despite receiving negative reviews from critics, who criticised the ageing Moore's performance, and Moore's own dislike of the film, it was a commercial success.

8.document_name: Wikipedia: A View to a Kill
8.content: The Duran Duran theme song "A View to a Kill" performed well in the charts, becoming the only Bond theme song to reach number one on the Billboard Hot 100 and earning a Golden Globe nomination for Best Song.

9.document_name: Wikipedia: A View to a Kill
9.content: The film was followed by The Living Daylights in 1987, with Timothy Dalton playing Bond.

10.document_name: Wikipedia: A View to a Kill
10.content:
== Plot ==
MI6 agent James Bond is sent to Siberia to locate the body of 003 and recover a Soviet microchip.

11.document_name: Wikipedia: A View to a Kill
11.content: Q analyzes the microchip, establishing it to be a copy of one designed to withstand an electromagnetic pulse, made by government contractor Zorin Industries.

12.document_name: Wikipedia: A View to a Kill
12.content: Bond visits Ascot Racecourse to observe the company's owner, Max Zorin.

13.document_name: Wikipedia: A View to a Kill
13.content: Sir Godfrey Tibbett, a racehorse trainer and MI6 agent, believes Zorin's horses, which win consistently, are drugged, although tests proved negative.

14.document_name: Wikipedia: A View to a Kill
14.content: Through Tibbett, Bond meets French private detective Achille Aubergine, who informs Bond that Zorin is holding a horse sale later in the month.

15.document_name: Wikipedia: A View to a Kill
15.content: During their dinner at the Eiffel Tower, Aubergine is killed by Zorin's bodyguard May Day, who subsequently escapes.

16.document_name: Wikipedia: A View to a Kill
16.content: Bond and Tibbett travel to Zorin's estate for the horse sale.

17.document_name: Wikipedia: A View to a Kill
17.content: Bond is puzzled by a woman who rebuffs him; he discovers Zorin has written her a cheque for $5 million.

18.document_name: Wikipedia: A View to a Kill
18.content: That night, Bond and Tibbett infiltrate Zorin's laboratory, where he is implanting adrenaline-releasing devices in his horses.

19.document_name: Wikipedia: A View to a Kill
19.content: Zorin identifies Bond as an agent, has May Day murder Tibbett, and attempts to have Bond killed.

40.content: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), also known as motor neuron disease (MND), Lou Gehrig's disease or Charcot's disease (English:  shar-KOH, French: [ʃaʁko]), is a rare terminal neurodegenerative disease defined by the progressive loss of both upper and lower motor neurons that normally control voluntary muscle contraction.

41.content: ALS is the most common of the motor neuron diseases.

42.content: ALS often presents with gradual muscle stiffness, twitches, weakness, and wasting.

43.content: Motor neuron loss typically continues until the ability to eat, speak, move, and breathe without mechanical support is lost.

44.content: At least 50% of people with ALS experience significant changes in thinking and behavior, with 15% of individuals going on to develop frontotemporal dementia.

45.content: An ALS diagnosis is made based on a person's signs and symptoms, with additional testing conducted to rule out other potential causes.

46.content: Depending on which areas of the body are affected first, ALS may be classified as limb-onset (beginning with weakness in the arms or legs) or bulbar-onset (beginning with difficulty in speaking or swallowing).

47.content: Respiratory onset occurs in approximately 1–3% of cases.

48.content: Most cases of ALS (about 90–95%) have no known cause and are known as sporadic ALS.

49.content: Genetic, autoimmune, and environmental factors are believed to be involved in the onset of ALS.

50.content: Approximately 5–10% of ALS cases have a known genetic cause and are often linked to a family history of ALS; such cases are known as familial ALS or hereditary ALS.

51.content: Mutations in the C9orf72 gene are the most common known genetic cause of familial ALS and are also found in a subset of sporadic cases.

52.content: Four disease-linked genes are responsible for approximately half of all genetic cases.

53.content: There is no known cure for ALS.

54.content: The goal of treatment is to slow the disease progression and improve symptoms.

55.content: FDA-approved treatments that slow the progression of ALS include riluzole and edaravone.

56.content: Non-invasive ventilation may result in both improved quality and length of life.

57.content: Mechanical ventilation can prolong survival but does not stop disease progression.

58.content: A feeding tube may help maintain weight and nutrition.

59.content: Death is usually caused by respiratory failure.

60.content: Catherine Elizabeth Deeley (born 23 October 1976) is an English television presenter.

61.content: Since 2024, she has co-presented ITV's This Morning, alongside Ben Shephard.

62.content: Deeley began her television career as a co-presenter of the ITV children's show SMTV Live (1998–2002), for which she won a BAFTA Children's Award, and its spin-off chart show CD:UK (1998–2005).

63.content: In 2003, she co-presented the talent show Fame Academy on BBC One and became the presenter of the ITV talent show Stars in Their Eyes.

64.content: Following the final series of Stars in Their Eyes in 2006, Deeley began hosting the reality competition show So You Think You Can Dance in the United States, for which she has been nominated five times for a Primetime Emmy.

65.content: Since 2003, Deeley has been a patron of London's Great Ormond Street Hospital for sick children.

66.content: In December 2009, she was made a UNICEF UK ambassador.

67.content:
== Early life ==
Deeley was born on 23 October 1976 at Sandwell General Hospital in West Bromwich, West Midlands.

68.content: She grew up in Birmingham, in nearby Sutton Coldfield and Great Barr.

69.content: She attended Grove Vale Junior School and Dartmouth High School in Great Barr, where she played the clarinet in the Sandwell Youth Concert Band.

70.content: Deeley then attended Bishop Vesey's Grammar School in Sutton Coldfield.

71.content:
== Career ==
At the age of 14, Deeley entered a regional edition of a BBC competition for The Clothes Show, in which she reached the national finals.

72.content: She was signed as a model under her nickname of "Cat" to make it easier for clients to rebook her.

73.content: She left full-time fashion modelling in 1997, following changes in her contract with Storm.

74.content: Deeley started to co-present the MTV chart show, Hitlist UK, with close friend Edith Bowman.

75.content: From 1998 until 2002, Deeley was co-host of the Saturday morning children's programme SM:TV Live, and hosted its spin-off programmes CD:UK (1998–2005) and CD:UK Hotshots.

76.content: On SM:TV Live, she often acted as an apparently slightly unwilling assistant whenever the show featured a guest appearance by a magician, participating in a number of different illusions.

77.content: In 2001, Deeley won a Children's BAFTA award and appeared in an episode of the BBC's Happiness.

78.content: In 2002, she appeared in a television advert for Marks and Spencer.

79.content: Other programmes she hosted include The Record of the Year, Fame Academy, The 2004 Brit Awards and Stars in Their Eyes, as well as a weekly broadcast on London's Capital FM and a BBC Choice series, Roadtripping, both with former MTV colleague Edith Bowman.

80.content: A Commonwealth realm is a sovereign state in the Commonwealth of Nations that has the same constitutional monarch and head of state as the other realms.

81.content: The current monarch is King Charles III.

82.content: Except for the United Kingdom, in each of the realms the monarch is represented by a governor-general.

83.content: The phrase Commonwealth realm is an informal description not used in any law.

84.content: As of 2026, there are 15 Commonwealth realms: Antigua and Barbuda, Australia and its external territories, The Bahamas, Belize, Canada, Grenada, Jamaica, the Realm of New Zealand, Papua New Guinea, Saint Kitts and Nevis, Saint Lucia, Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, Solomon Islands, Tuvalu, and the United Kingdom and its territories.

85.content: While the Commonwealth of Nations has 56 independent member states, only these 15 have Charles III as head of state.

86.content: He is also Head of the Commonwealth, a ceremonial role.

87.content: The notion of these states sharing the same person as their monarch traces back to 1867 when Canada became the first "dominion": a largely self-governing nation that was nevertheless a part of the British Empire.

88.content: Others, such as Australia (1901) and New Zealand (1907), followed.

89.content: With the growing independence of the dominions in the 1920s, the Balfour Declaration of 1926 established the Commonwealth of Nations and that the nations were considered "equal in status ...

90.content: though united by a common allegiance to the Crown".

91.content: The Statute of Westminster 1931 further set the terms: of the relationship between the realms; and of their broader sharing of the monarch, including a convention that any alteration to the line of succession in any one country must be voluntarily approved by all the others.

92.content: After the significant and costly mutual defence assistance provided by empire nations during the Second World War, the modern Commonwealth of Nations was formally constituted by the London Declaration.

93.content: In 1950, India became a republic without leaving the Commonwealth.

94.content: This left seven independent nations sharing the Crown: Australia, Canada, Ceylon (now Sri Lanka), New Zealand, Pakistan, South Africa, and the United Kingdom.

95.content: Since then, new realms have been created as former colonies and dependencies have gained independence.

96.content: Saint Kitts and Nevis is the youngest extant realm, having achieved independence—while retaining the monarch—in 1983.

97.content: Some former realms have transitioned to presidential republics: most recently, Barbados changed from realm to republic in 2021.

98.content:
== List ==
There are currently 15 Commonwealth realms across three continents (nine in North America, five in Oceania, and one, the UK, in Europe).

99.content: Together, these realms have a population of more than 150 million and a combined land area of 18.7 million km2 (7.2 million sq mi).

100.content: The Cretaceous (IPA:  krih-TAY-shəss) is a geological period that lasted from about 143.1 to 66 Ma (million years ago).

101.content: It is the third and final period of the Mesozoic Era, as well as the longest.

102.content: At around 77.1 million years, it is the ninth and longest geological period of the entire Phanerozoic.

103.content: The name is derived from the Latin creta, 'chalk', which is abundant in deposits from the latter half of the period.

104.content: It is usually abbreviated K, for its German translation Kreide.

105.content: The Cretaceous was a period with a relatively warm climate, resulting in high eustatic sea levels that created numerous shallow inland seas.

106.content: These oceans and seas were populated with now-extinct marine reptiles, ammonites and rudists; while on land, dinosaurs continued to dominate.

107.content: The world was largely ice-free – although there is some evidence of brief periods of glaciation during the cooler first half – and forests extended to the poles.

108.content: Many of the dominant taxonomic groups present in modern times can be ultimately traced back to origins in the Cretaceous.

109.content: During this time, new groups of mammals and birds appeared, including the earliest relatives of placentals and marsupials (Eutheria and Metatheria respectively), with the earliest crown group birds appearing towards the end of the Cretaceous.

110.content: Teleost fish, the most diverse group of modern vertebrates, continued to diversify during the Cretaceous with the appearance of their most diverse subgroup Acanthomorpha during this period.

111.content: During the Early Cretaceous, flowering plants appeared and began to rapidly diversify, becoming the dominant group of plants across the Earth by the end of the Cretaceous, coincident with the decline and extinction of previously widespread gymnosperm groups.

112.content: The Cretaceous (along with the Mesozoic) ended with the Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction event, a large mass extinction in which many groups, including non-avian dinosaurs, pterosaurs, and large marine reptiles, died out; it is widely thought to have been caused by the impact of a large asteroid that formed the Chicxulub crater in the Gulf of Mexico.

113.content: The end of the Cretaceous is defined by the abrupt Cretaceous–Paleogene boundary (K–Pg boundary), a geologic signature associated with the mass extinction that lies between the Mesozoic and Cenozoic Eras.

114.content:
== Etymology and history ==
The Cretaceous as a separate period was first defined by Belgian geologist Jean d'Omalius d'Halloy in 1822 as the Terrain Crétacé, using strata in the Paris Basin and named for the extensive beds of chalk (calcium carbonate deposited by the shells of marine invertebrates, principally coccoliths), found in the upper Cretaceous of Western Europe.

115.content: The name 'Cretaceous' was derived from the Latin creta, meaning 'chalk'.

116.content: The twofold division of the Cretaceous was implemented by Conybeare and Phillips in 1822.

117.content: Alcide d'Orbigny in 1840 divided the French Cretaceous into five étages (stages): the Neocomian, Aptian, Albian, Turonian, and Senonian, later adding the Urgonian between Neocomian and Aptian and the Cenomanian between the Albian and Turonian.

118.content:
== Geology ==


=== Subdivisions ===
The Cretaceous is divided into Early and Late Cretaceous epochs, or Lower and Upper Cretaceous series.

119.content: In older literature, the Cretaceous is sometimes divided into three series: Neocomian (lower/early), Gallic (middle) and Senonian (upper/late).

120.content: Croatia, officially the Republic of Croatia, is a country in Central and Southeastern Europe, on the coast of the Adriatic Sea.

121.content: It borders Slovenia to the northwest, Hungary to the northeast, Serbia to the east, Bosnia and Herzegovina and Montenegro to the southeast, and shares a maritime border with Italy to the west.

122.content: The Croatian archipelago contains over 1,000 islands and islets, the largest overseas territory on the Adriatic Sea.

123.content: Its capital, largest city and main cultural and economic centre is Zagreb.

124.content: Major urban centers include Split, Rijeka, and Osijek.

125.content: The country is composed of twenty counties spanning 56,594 square kilometres (21,851 square miles) within four historical and cultural regions.

126.content: Croatia has a population of nearly 3.9 million as of 2026.

127.content: Croatian history began with the 6th century arrival of the Croats to Roman Illyria.

128.content: Settled as two duchies a century later, Croatia was granted independence in 878 under Duke Branimir and elevated into a kingdom under King Tomislav in 925.

129.content: The Trpimirović dynastic succession crisis placed Croatia into a personal union with Hungary in 1102.

130.content: In 1527, amid Ottoman conflict, Croatia aligned with the Habsburg monarchy.

131.content: It reorganized into the State of Slovenes, Croats, and Serbs before merging into the Kingdom of Yugoslavia in 1918.

132.content: During World War II, most of Croatia was invaded by the Axis powers who installed a puppet state known as the Independent State of Croatia.

133.content: A resistance movement restored sovereignty, emerging as the Socialist Republic of Croatia within the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in 1943.

134.content: Croatia declared independence from Yugoslavia in 1991, successfully fighting the War of Independence until 1995.

135.content: Modern Croatia is a representative democracy with a prime minister, president, and unicameral parliament.

136.content: Its constitution ensures separation of powers between the executive, legislative, and judicial branches.

137.content: Croatian politics reflect a multi-party system.

138.content: Croatia is part of many international organizations and forums including the European Union, United Nations, WTO, and NATO, among others.

139.content: It exerts regional influence as a small power in Europe, particularly within neighboring Southeast Europe.

140.content: Despicable Me 2 is a 2013 American animated comedy film directed by Chris Renaud and Pierre Coffin, and written by Cinco Paul and Ken Daurio.

141.content: Produced by Universal Pictures and Illumination Entertainment, it is the second installment in the Despicable Me franchise following the 2010 film.

142.content: The film stars the voices of Steve Carell, Kristen Wiig, Benjamin Bratt, Russell Brand, Miranda Cosgrove,  Steve Coogan, and Ken Jeong.

143.content: In the film, secret agent Lucy Wilde (Wiig) recruits retired supervillain Gru to investigate the theft of a powerful mutagen by an unknown criminal suspected by the latter to be El Macho (Bratt), a villain who is believed to have died decades prior.

144.content: Development of Despicable Me 2 began in 2010 following the success of the original film, with the directors, producers, and writers returning.

145.content: Production was underway by February 2012, with the majority of the cast returning to voice the characters, along with new cast members, while animation services were provided by Illumination Mac Guff in France.

146.content: Al Pacino was cast as the voice of El Macho, recording all of his dialogue, but left in May 2013 over creative differences; Bratt was brought in to replace Pacino, and used him as an inspiration after finding imitating his voice impossible.

147.content: Heitor Pereira and Pharrell Williams returned for the sequel's music.

148.content: Despicable Me 2 premiered in Australia on June 5, 2013, and was theatrically released in the United States on July 3 by Universal Pictures.

149.content: It received generally positive reviews from critics, who praised its humor and animation.

150.content: It earned $971 million worldwide, becoming the third-highest-grossing film of 2013 and the most profitable film for Universal at the time.

151.content: It was nominated for two awards at the 86th Academy Awards, and received numerous other accolades.

152.content: A sequel, Despicable Me 3, was released in 2017.

153.content:
== Plot ==
A mysterious aircraft steals a highly potent mutagen known as PX-41 from a laboratory in the Arctic Circle.

154.content: Silas Ramsbottom, director of the Anti-Villain League (AVL), sends agent Lucy Wilde to recruit former supervillain Gru.

155.content: Gru refuses and informs Silas and Lucy that he has enough responsibilities as a father and as the owner of a jelly-producing business.

157.content: Nefario is forced to retire and accept a job offer to assist another villain, which convinces Gru to work with the AVL after all.

158.content: He and Lucy are stationed at a shopping center, with a cupcake store as their front.

159.content: Gru suspects that Mexican restaurant owner Eduardo Pérez might be "El Macho", a supervillain who was presumed dead twenty years ago after riding a shark into an active volcano with 250 pounds of dynamite strapped to his chest.

180.content: A floppy disk, diskette, or floppy diskette is a type of disk storage made from a thin, flexible disk coated with a magnetic storage medium.

181.content: It is enclosed in a square or nearly square plastic shell lined with fabric to help remove dust from the spinning disk.

182.content: Floppy disks store digital data, which can be read or written when inserted into a floppy disk drive (FDD) connected to or built into a computer or other device.

183.content: The three most popular formats of floppy disks (and their drives) are the 8-inch, 5¼-inch, and 3½-inch versions.

184.content: The first floppy disks, invented and made by IBM in 1971, had a disk diameter of 8 inches (200 mm).

185.content: Subsequently, the 5¼-inch (130 mm) and then the 3½-inch (90 mm) became a ubiquitous form of data storage and data transfer into the first years of the 21st century.

186.content: By the end of the 1980s, 5¼-inch (130 mm) disks had been superseded by 3½-inch (90 mm) disks.

187.content: During this time, PCs frequently came equipped with drives of both sizes.

188.content: By the mid-1990s, 5¼-inch drives had virtually disappeared, the 3½-inch disk became the dominant format.

189.content: The advantages of the 3½-inch (90 mm) disk were its higher capacity, smaller physical size, and its rigid case which provided better protection from dirt and other environmental risks.

190.content: Floppy disks were so common in late 20th-century culture that many electronic and software programs continue to use save icons that look like floppy disks well into the 21st century, as a form of skeuomorphic design.

191.content: While floppy disk drives still have some limited uses, especially with legacy industrial computer equipment, they have been superseded by data storage methods with much greater data storage capacity and data transfer speed, such as USB flash drives, memory cards, optical discs, and storage available through local computer networks and cloud storage.

192.content:
== Categories ==

Industry observers categorize floppy disks and floppy disk drives according to size and capacity with four major categories being 8 inches (200 mm), 5.25 inches (130 mm), 3.5 inches (90 mm) and high-capacity floppy disks and floppy disk drives.

193.content: There were in addition, variant products that did not fit these categories.

194.content: The distinguishing characteristic between the high-capacity products and their lower capacity brethren, frequently categorized as standard floppies, was the use of servomechanisms to increase the number of tracks and thereby increase capacity.

195.content: The four categories each represented generations; from the beginning each generation had substantially greater market success and ultimately succeeded the previous one, but the high-capacity floppy generation, although having some success, was never as successful as the prior 3½-inch (90 mm) generation, and became essentially obsolete by 2011.

196.content: While the original IBM 8-inch (200 mm) disk was actually so defined, the other sizes are defined in millimeters, their names being but rough approximations.

197.content: Different sizes of floppy disks are mechanically incompatible, and disks can fit only one size of drive.

198.content: Drive assemblies with both 3.5 inches (90 mm) and 5.25 inches (130 mm) slots were available during the transition period between the sizes, but they contained two separate drive mechanisms.

199.content: As computer platforms began to form, attempts were made at interchangeability.

200.content: Gal Gadot (Hebrew: גל גדות, pronounced [ˈɡal ɡaˈdot]; born 30 April 1985) is an Israeli actress.

201.content: She gained recognition for portraying Wonder Woman in the DC Extended Universe films (2016–2023).

202.content: In 2018, Gadot was named one of Time's 100 most influential people in the world and ranked by Forbes as the tenth–highest-paid actress, later rising to third-highest in 2020.

203.content: In 2025, she became the first Israeli actor to receive a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame.

204.content: Gadot grew up in Rosh HaAyin and first gained attention locally after winning Miss Israel 2004, followed by two years of mandatory service in the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) as a combat trainer.

205.content: During this time, she participated in a Maxim photo shoot that boosted her public profile, leading her to begin modeling and endorsing various brands.

206.content: Shortly after, she made her television debut in the Israeli drama Bubot in 2008, followed by her film debut in a supporting role as Gisele Yashar in Fast & Furious (2009), reprising it in multiple sequels (2011–2023).

207.content: She also appeared on Israeli television in the second season of Asfur (2010–2012) and later in Kathmandu (2012).

208.content: Gadot first portrayed Wonder Woman in Batman v Superman: Dawn of Justice (2016).

209.content: The success of the film led to her starring in Wonder Woman (2017), which became a major box office hit.

210.content: She reprised the role again in Justice League (2017) and Wonder Woman 1984 (2020), the latter of which she co-produced.

211.content: Since then, she has starred in Red Notice (2021), Death on the Nile (2022), and Heart of Stone (2023), which she co-produced.

212.content: In 2025 she portrayed the Evil Queen in Snow White and Gemma Donati in In the Hand of Dante.

213.content: Beyond acting, Gadot and her husband have co-founded a film production company, launched a food brand, and invested in Israeli startups.

214.content: Gadot is widely celebrated in Israel as a national icon and ambassador and has been honored by various Jewish and Zionist organizations for her effect on Israel's image, including the Israeli-American Council (IAC), Anti-Defamation League (ADL), Jerusalem Film Festival, and Hadassah.

215.content: She has also been awarded a Genesis Prize.

216.content: Her support for the Israeli military and for hostages held in the Gaza Strip has drawn criticism from Palestinian nationalists, as well as from some pro-Israeli nationalists who argue she has not shown strong support.

217.content:
== Early life ==
Gadot was born on 30 April 1985 in Petah Tikva, where she initially lived at Stampfer street.

218.content: She was born to Jewish parents of Ashkenazi descent; her mother's roots are Czech and Polish, while her father's are Austrian, Russian, and German.

219.content: Her parents, Michael, an engineer, and Irit, a physical education teacher, Hebraized their surname from "Greenstein" to "Gadot" before her birth.

220.content: Galactic empires are a science fiction setting trope, in which most or all of the habitable planets in the setting's galaxy are ruled by a single centralized political entity.

221.content: Galactic empires most frequently appear in works in the sub-genres of science fantasy and space opera, although they may appear in other sub-genres as well.

222.content: Works featuring galactic empires may have them as the story's focus, chronicling the empire's growth and/or decline.

223.content: Alternatively, they may merely serve as a backdrop against which the events of the story play out.

224.content:
== Notable examples ==


=== Foundation ===
Galactic empires are in many cases consciously modeled on historical Earth-bound empires.

225.content: Asimov stated explicitly that the Galactic Empire whose fall is depicted in his Foundation books is also modeled on the Roman Empire, with the author taking direct inspiration from the historical writings of Edward Gibbon, even to the point of basing some individual characters on historical figures.

226.content: Specifically, Pebble in the Sky, which is set on Earth – a poor and backward province of the Galactic Empire – is modeled on Roman-ruled Judea in the 1st century AD.

227.content: Asimov's Earth – like the historical Judea – is sharply polarized between those who accept the Imperial authority and the fanatic "Zealots" who hatch violent plots of bloody rebellion and are the book's clear villains.

228.content:
=== Star Wars ===

240.content: Hugh Michael Jackman (born 12 October 1968) is an Australian actor, singer, and producer.

241.content: Prominent on both screen and stage, he has received various accolades, including a Primetime Emmy Award, a Grammy Award and two Tony Awards, along with nominations for an Academy Award and a British Academy Film Award.

242.content: Jackman was appointed a Companion of the Order of Australia in 2019.

243.content: Jackman's breakthrough role came as Wolverine, having portrayed him across the X-Men film franchise and in the Marvel Cinematic Universe from X-Men (2000) to Deadpool & Wolverine (2024).

244.content: As a leading man, he found further success with roles in films such as Kate & Leopold (2001), Van Helsing (2004), The Prestige (2006), Australia (2008), Real Steel (2011), Prisoners (2013), The Greatest Showman (2017), Bad Education (2019), Song Sung Blue (2025), and The Sheep Detectives (2026).

245.content: For his role as Jean Valjean in the musical Les Misérables (2012), he was nominated for the Academy Award for Best Actor and won a Golden Globe Award for Best Actor.

246.content: For The Greatest Showman soundtrack, Jackman received a Grammy Award for Best Compilation Soundtrack.

247.content: He also provided voice roles in the animated films Flushed Away and  Happy Feet (both 2006), Rise of the Guardians (2012) and Missing Link (2019).

248.content: Jackman is also known for his early theatre roles in the original Australian productions of Beauty and the Beast as Gaston in 1995 and Sunset Boulevard as Joe Gillis in 1996.

249.content: He earned a Laurence Olivier Award nomination for his performance as Curly McLain in the West End revival of Oklahoma!

250.content: In 2002, he made his American stage debut in a concert of Carousel as Billy Bigelow at Carnegie Hall.

251.content: On Broadway, he won the 2004 Tony Award and Drama Desk Award for Best Actor in a Musical for his role of Peter Allen in The Boy from Oz.

252.content: From 2021 to 2023, Jackman starred as con man Harold Hill in the Broadway revival of the musical The Music Man, earning another Tony Award nomination.

253.content: A four-time host of the Tony Awards, he won an Emmy Award for hosting the 2005 ceremony.

254.content: He also hosted the 81st Academy Awards in 2009.

255.content:
== Early life ==
Jackman was born in Sydney, New South Wales, to English parents Grace McNeil (née Greenwood) and Christopher John Jackman (1936–2021), a Cambridge-educated accountant.

256.content: His parents moved to Australia in 1967 as part of the "Ten Pound Poms" immigration scheme.

257.content: Thus, in addition to his Australian citizenship, Jackman holds British citizenship by virtue of being born to UK-born parents.

258.content: One of his paternal great-grandfathers, Nicholas Isidor Bellas, was Greek, from the Ottoman Empire (now in Greece).

259.content: His parents were devout Christians, having been converted by Evangelist Billy Graham after their marriage.

260.content: Kellyanne Elizabeth Conway (née Fitzpatrick; born  January 20, 1967) is an American political consultant and pollster who served as senior counselor to the president in the first presidency of Donald Trump from 2017 to 2020.

261.content: She was previously Trump's campaign manager, having been appointed in August 2016; Conway is the first woman to have run a successful U.S.

263.content: She previously held roles as a campaign manager and strategist in the Republican Party and was formerly president and CEO of the Polling Company/WomanTrend.

264.content: In the 2016 Republican Party presidential primaries, Conway endorsed Ted Cruz and chaired a pro-Cruz political action committee until Cruz later dropped out of the race.

265.content: In July 2016, after Cruz dropped out the race, Trump appointed Conway as a senior advisor and later campaign manager.

266.content: On December 22, 2016, Trump announced that Conway would join his administration as counselor to the president.

267.content: On November 29, 2017, Attorney General Jeff Sessions announced that Conway would oversee White House efforts to combat the opioid overdose epidemic.

268.content: In Conway's role as senior counselor to the president, she used the phrase "alternative facts" to describe fictitious attendance numbers for Trump's inauguration.

269.content: In 2017, members of Congress from both parties called for an investigation of an alleged ethics violation after she publicly endorsed commercial products associated with the president's daughter, Ivanka Trump.

271.content: Office of Special Counsel recommended that Conway be fired for "unprecedented" multiple violations of the Hatch Act of 1939, but she was not fired.

272.content: In August 2020, Conway left the administration.

273.content: Conway is a frequent media commentator.

274.content: In 2022, she joined Fox News as a contributor, and she appears as a guest or host on a variety of programs, including Hannity, The Five, Outnumbered, The Big Weekend Show, and others.

275.content: She also contributed to Fox's 2022 midterm election coverage.

276.content: In July 2024, Fox News announced that Conway would begin to host a weekly program on the network's streaming platform, Fox Nation, called Here's The Deal with Kellyanne Conway.

277.content:

279.content: Conway's parents divorced when she was three, and she was raised by her mother, grandmother, and two unmarried aunts in Atco.

300.content: Libya, officially the State of Libya, is a country in the Maghreb region of North Africa.

301.content: It borders the Mediterranean Sea to the north, Egypt to the east, Sudan to the southeast, Chad to the south, Niger to the southwest, Algeria to the west, and Tunisia to the northwest.

302.content: With an area of almost 1.8 million km2 (700,000 sq mi), Libya is the fourth-largest country in Africa and the Arab world, and the 16th-largest in the world.

303.content: The country claims 32,000 square kilometres of southeastern Algeria, south of the Libyan town of Ghat.

304.content: The capital and largest city is Tripoli, located in the northwest and containing over a million of Libya's seven million people.

305.content: Libya has been inhabited by Berbers since the late Bronze Age as descendants from Iberomaurusian and Capsian cultures.

306.content: In classical antiquity, the Phoenicians established city-states and trading posts in western Libya, while several Greek cities were established in the East.

307.content: Parts of Libya were variously ruled by Carthaginians, Numidians, Persians, and Greeks before the entire region became a part of the Roman Empire.

308.content: Libya was an early centre of Christianity.

309.content: After the fall of the Western Roman Empire, the area of Libya was mostly occupied by the Vandals until the 7th century when invasions brought Islam to the region.

310.content: From then on, centuries of Arab migration to the Maghreb shifted the demographic scope of Libya in favour of Arabs.

311.content: In the 16th century, the Spanish Empire and the Knights Hospitaller occupied Tripoli until Ottoman rule began in 1551.

312.content: Libya was involved in the Barbary Wars of the 18th and 19th centuries.

313.content: Ottoman rule continued until the Italo-Turkish War in 1911, which resulted in Italy occupying Libya and establishing two colonies: Italian Tripolitania and Italian Cyrenaica, later unified in the Italian Libya colony from 1934 to 1943.

314.content: During World War II, Libya was an area of warfare in the North African Campaign.

315.content: The Italian population then went into decline and Libya became independent as a kingdom in 1951.

316.content: A bloodless military coup in 1969, initiated by a coalition led by Colonel Muammar Gaddafi, overthrew King Idris I and created a republic.

317.content: Gaddafi was often described by critics as a dictator, and was one of the world's longest serving non-royal leaders.

318.content: He ruled for 42 years until being overthrown and killed in the 2011 civil war, which was part of the wider Arab Spring, with authority transferred to the National Transitional Council then to the elected General National Congress.

319.content: Since 2011, Libya has been involved in a political and humanitarian crisis, and by 2014, two rival authorities claimed to govern Libya, which led to a second civil war, with parts of Libya split between separate governments, based in Tripoli and Tobruk, as well as various tribal and Islamist militias.

320.content: Macedonia (  MASS-ih-DOH-nee-ə) is a geographical and historical region of the Balkan Peninsula in Southeast Europe.

321.content: The modern region at its maximum extent is considered to span the largest part of northern Greece, known as Greek Macedonia, all of North Macedonia, a large part of southwestern Bulgaria, known as Pirin Macedonia, and small parts of Albania, Serbia, and Kosovo.

322.content: In classical antiquity, the kingdom of Macedon rose into an empire under Alexander the Great during the second half of the 4th century BC, signaling the start of the Hellenistic period.

323.content: In the 2nd century BC Macedonia became a province of the Roman empire.

324.content: During the medieval period, a Byzantine theme under the name of Macedonia was carved out mostly in Thrace.

325.content: Macedonia came to be defined by European authors as the modern geographical region by the mid-19th century while under Ottoman rule.

326.content:
== Etymology ==

Both proper nouns Makedṓn and Makednós are morphologically derived from the Ancient Greek adjective makednós meaning "tall, slim", and are related to the term Macedonia.

327.content:
== Boundaries and Terminology ==

Prior to its expansion under Philip II, the ancient kingdom of Macedonia, to which the modern region owes its name, lay within the central and western parts of the current Greek province of Macedonia.

328.content: The Roman province of Macedonia consisted of what is today northern and central Greece, much of the geographical area of the Republic of North Macedonia and southeast Albania.

329.content: In late Roman times, the provincial boundaries were reorganized to form the Diocese of Macedonia, consisting of most of modern mainland Greece, Crete, southern Albania, southwest Bulgaria, and most of Republic of North Macedonia.

330.content: In the Byzantine Empire, a province under the name of Macedonia was carved out of the original Theme of Thrace, which was well east of the Struma River.

331.content: This thema variously included parts of Thrace and gave its name to the Macedonian dynasty.

332.content: Hence, Byzantine documents of this era that mention Macedonia are most probably referring to the Macedonian theme.

333.content: The parts of Macedonia, on the other hand, which were ruled by the First Bulgarian Empire throughout the 9th and the 10th century, were incorporated into the Byzantine Empire in 1018 as the Themе of Bulgaria.

334.content: With the gradual conquest of southeastern Europe by the Ottomans in the late 14th century, the name of Macedonia disappeared as an administrative designation for several centuries and was rarely displayed on maps.

335.content: The name was again revived to mean a distinct geographical region in the 19th century, defining the region bounded by Mount Olympus, the Pindus range, mounts Shar and Osogovo, the western Rhodopes, the lower course of the river Mesta (Greek Nestos) and the Aegean Sea, developing roughly the same borders that it has today.

336.content:
== History ==


=== Neolithic period ===
While Macedonia shows signs of human habitation as old as the Paleolithic period (among which is the Petralona cave with the oldest European humanoid), the earliest known settlements, such as Nea Nikomedeia in Imathia (today's Greek Macedonia), date back 9,000 years.

337.content: The houses at Nea Nikomedeia were constructed—as were most structures throughout the Neolithic in northern Greece—of wattle and daub on a timber frame.

338.content: The cultural assemblage includes well-made pottery in simple shapes with occasional decoration in white on a red background, clay female figurines of the 'rod-headed' type known from Thessaly to the Danube Valley, stone axes and adzes, chert blades, and ornaments of stone including curious 'nose plugs' of uncertain function.

339.content: The assemblage of associated objects differs from one house to the next, suggesting some degree of craft specialisation had already been established from the beginning of the site's history.

344.content: NRG Recording Studios is a recording facility located in North Hollywood, California, that was created by producer and mixer Jay Baumgardner in 1992.

349.content: The studio evolved from handling TV gigs like The Dolly Parton Show to becoming a hub for various music genres, particularly country and Christian music.

355.content: Paramore is an American rock band formed in Franklin, Tennessee, in 2004.

356.content: Since 2017, the band's lineup has included lead vocalist Hayley Williams, guitarist Taylor York, and drummer Zac Farro.

357.content: Williams and Farro are the founding members of the group, while York, a high school friend of the original lineup, joined in 2007.

358.content: The band was signed to Fueled by Ramen, a subsidiary of Atlantic Records.

359.content: Williams was signed to Atlantic separately, as she was scouted when she was a teenager.

360.content: They were the only label to let her stay in the band instead of going solo, but Atlantic said the rest of the band had to sign to Fueled by Ramen.

361.content: The group's debut album, All We Know Is Falling (2005), reached  number 30 on Billboard's Heatseekers Chart in 2006 and number four on the UK Rock Chart in 2009.

363.content: (2007) became a mainstream success thanks to the success of the singles "Misery Business", "Crushcrushcrush", and "That's What You Get".

364.content: The album was certified Platinum in the US and the band received a Best New Artist nomination at the 2008 Grammy Awards.

365.content: Their 2009 follow-up, Brand New Eyes, reached number two on the Billboard 200 and became the band's second-highest-charting album to date.

366.content: It produced the top-forty single "The Only Exception" and went platinum in Ireland and the UK.

367.content: Following the departure of Zac and Josh Farro in 2010, the band released their self-titled fourth album in 2013.

368.content: Paramore gave the band their first number one album on the US Billboard 200 and was also the number one album in the UK, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand, Brazil, Argentina and Mexico.

369.content: It included the singles "Still Into You" and "Ain't It Fun", with the latter winning the Grammy Award for Best Rock Song for Williams and York as songwriters, making it Paramore's first Grammy win.

370.content: The band's lineup changed once again after this album, with bassist Jeremy Davis leaving the band near the end of 2015 and former drummer Zac Farro rejoining the band in 2017.

371.content: Their albums After Laughter (2017) and This Is Why (2023) peaked within the top-ten, the latter of which won the Grammy Award for Best Rock Album.

372.content:
== History ==


=== 2002–2004: Formation and early years ===
In 2002, at age 13, vocalist Hayley Williams moved from her hometown Meridian, Mississippi, to Franklin, Tennessee, where she met brothers Josh Farro and Zac Farro at a weekly supplemental program for home-schooled students.

373.content: Shortly after arriving, she began taking vocal lessons with Brett Manning.

374.content: Prior to forming Paramore, Williams and bassist Jeremy Davis, along with friend Kimee Read, took part in a funk cover band called The Factory, while Josh and Zac Farro had practiced together after school.

375.content: Pearl Jam is an American rock band from Seattle, Washington, that formed in 1990.

376.content: One of the key bands in the grunge movement of the early 1990s, Pearl Jam has outsold and outlasted many of its contemporaries and is considered one of the most influential bands from that decade.

377.content: The band has consisted of guitarists Stone Gossard and Mike McCready, bassist Jeff Ament, and vocalist and guitarist Eddie Vedder since its formation.

378.content: The band had a revolving cast of drummers throughout their early days, including Dave Krusen, Matt Chamberlain, Dave Abbruzzese, and Jack Irons.

379.content: The band's longest-tenured drummer was Matt Cameron, who joined the band in 1998 and departed in 2025.

380.content: Keyboardist Boom Gaspar has also featured with the band as a session and touring musician since 2002.

381.content: Formed after the demise of Gossard and Ament's previous bands, Green River and Mother Love Bone, Pearl Jam broke into the mainstream with their debut album Ten (1991).

382.content: Ten stayed on the US Billboard 200 chart for nearly five years, and has gone on to become one of the highest-selling rock albums ever, being certified 13× platinum by the Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA).

383.content: Released in 1993, Pearl Jam's second album, Vs., sold over 950,378 copies in its first week of release, setting the record for most copies of an album sold in its first week of release at the time.

384.content: Their third album, Vitalogy (1994), became the second-fastest-selling CD in history at the time, with more than 877,000 units sold in its first week.

385.content: Pearl Jam's members often shunned popular music industry practices such as making music videos or participating in interviews.

386.content: The band unsuccessfully sued Ticketmaster in 1994, claiming it had monopolized the concert-ticket market.

387.content: In 2006, Rolling Stone described the band as having "spent much of the past decade deliberately tearing apart their own fame".

388.content: Pearl Jam had sold more than 100 million albums worldwide, including nearly 32 million albums in the United States by 2012, making them one of the best-selling bands of all time.

389.content: Pearl Jam was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2017 in its first year of eligibility.

390.content: They were ranked eighth in a readers' poll by Rolling Stone magazine in its "Top Ten Live Acts of All Time" issue.

391.content: Throughout its career, the band has promoted wider social and political issues, such as abortion rights sentiments and opposition to George W.

392.content: Bush's presidency, with Vedder acting as its spokesman on these issues.

414.content: Sancho Panza (; Spanish: [ˈsantʃo ˈpanθa]) is a fictional character in the novel Don Quixote written by Spanish author Miguel de Cervantes Saavedra in 1605.

415.content: Sancho acts as squire to Don Quixote and provides comments throughout the novel, known as sanchismos, that are a combination of broad humour, ironic Spanish proverbs, and earthy wit.

417.content: English "paunch", Italian pancia, several Italian dialects panza, Portuguese and Galician pança, French panse, Romanian pântec, Catalan panxa).

418.content:
== Don Quixote ==

Before a fit of madness turned Alonso Quijano into Don Quixote, Sancho Panza was indeed his servant.

419.content: When the novel begins, Sancho has been married for a long time to a woman named Teresa Cascajo and has a daughter, María Sancha (also named Marisancha, Marica, María, Sancha, and Sanchica), who is said to be old enough to be married.

420.content: Sancho's wife is described more or less as a feminine version of Sancho, both in looks and behaviour.

421.content: When Don Quixote proposes Sancho to be his squire, neither he nor his family strongly oppose it.

422.content: Sancho is illiterate and proud of it but by influence of his new master, he develops considerable knowledge about some books.

423.content: Sancho provides the earthy wisdom of Spanish proverbs, surprising his master.

424.content: During the travels with Don Quixote, he keeps contact with his wife by dictating letters addressed to her.

425.content: Sancho Panza offers interpolated narrative voice throughout the tale, a literary convention invented by Cervantes.

426.content: Sancho Panza is precursor to "the sidekick," and is symbolic of practicality over idealism.

427.content: Sancho is the everyman, who, though not sharing his master's delusional "enchantment" until late in the novel, remains his ever-faithful companion realist, and functions as the clever sidekick.

428.content: Salvador de Madariaga detected that, as the book progresses, there is a "Quixotization" of Sancho and a "Sanchification" of Don Quixote, so much that, when the knight recovers sanity on his deathbed, it is Sancho who tries to convince him to become pastoral shepherds.

429.content: In the novel, Don Quixote comments on the historical state and condition of Aragón and Castilla, which are vying for power in Europe.

430.content: Sancho Panza represents, among other things, the quintessentially Spanish brand of skepticism of the period.

431.content: Sancho obediently follows his master, despite being sometimes puzzled by Quixote's actions.

432.content: Riding a donkey, he helps Quixote get out of various conflicts while looking forward to rewards of aventura that Quixote tells him of.

433.content:
== Don Quixote, Part Two ==


=== Sancho's name ===
Cervantes variously names Sancho in the first book Sancho Zancas (legs); however, in the second book, he standardizes Sancho's name in reply to the "false" Avellaneda Quixote sequel.

474.content: The Outsiders is the fourth studio album by American country music artist Eric Church.

477.content:
It was before the release that Church received media attention for saying "I think genres are dead."

494.content: Uranium-235 (235U or U-235) is an isotope of uranium making up about 0.72% of natural uranium.

495.content: Unlike the predominant isotope uranium-238, it is fissile, i.e., it can sustain a nuclear chain reaction.

496.content: It is the only fissile isotope that exists in nature as a primordial nuclide and was discovered in 1935 by Arthur Jeffrey Dempster.

497.content: The release of energy from the fission of Uranium-235 powers most nuclear reactors and nuclear weapons.

498.content: Uranium enrichment is the process of taking natural uranium and increasing the proportion of uranium-235.

499.content: Some reactor types can use natural uranium directly, while nuclear weapons and some others reactor types require uranium enriched in U-235.

500.content: Uranium-235 has a half-life of 704 million years.

501.content: Its fission cross section for slow thermal neutrons is about 584.3±1 barns.

502.content: For fast neutrons it is on the order of 1 barn.

503.content: Most neutron absorptions induce fission, though a minority (about 15%) result in the formation of uranium-236.

504.content:
== Fission properties ==

The fission of one atom of uranium-235 releases 202.5 MeV (3.24×10−11 J) inside the reactor.

505.content: That corresponds to 19.54 TJ/mol, or 83.14 TJ/kg.

506.content: Another 8.8 MeV escapes the reactor as anti-neutrinos.

507.content:
When 23592U nuclei are bombarded with neutrons, one of the many fission reactions that it can undergo is the following (shown in the adjacent image):

Heavy water reactors and some graphite moderated reactors can use natural uranium, but light water reactors must use low enriched uranium because of the higher neutron absorption of light water.

508.content: Uranium enrichment removes some of the uranium-238 and increases the proportion of uranium-235.

509.content: Highly enriched uranium (HEU), which contains an even greater proportion of uranium-235, is sometimes used in the reactors of nuclear submarines, research reactors and nuclear weapons.

510.content: Each fission of Uranium-235 releases an average of 2.43 neutrons, most commonly two or three.

511.content: If at least one neutron from uranium-235 fission strikes another nucleus and causes it to fission, then the chain reaction will continue.

512.content: If the reaction continues to sustain itself, it is said to be critical, and the mass of 235U required to produce the critical condition is said to be a critical mass.

513.content: A critical chain reaction can be achieved at low concentrations of 235U if the neutrons from fission are moderated to lower their speed, since the probability for fission with slow neutrons is greater.

514.content: "Victoria" is a song by the New Zealand rock band The Exponents from the band's 1983 album Prayers Be Answered.

515.content: Released in June 1982 as the band's first single, it reached Number 6 on the New Zealand singles chart.

516.content: The song was selected by a panel of New Zealand songwriters to have been the #8 top 100 New Zealand songs of all time.

517.content:
== Background ==
"Victoria" was inspired by Jordan Luck's landlady in Christchurch, with the name Victoria used as a pseudonym (her real name was Vicky).

518.content: She successfully ran an escort agency but lived with an abusive man: Luck questioned her relationship with the line "What do you see in him?".

519.content: "Victoria was 23 and earned [sic] the whole apartment block.

521.content: And yes, she read Alvin Toffler.

522.content:
But we'd wake up in the morning and she'd be bruised because her boyfriend was beating her up." 
The band moved to Auckland before the release of the song.

523.content: After the single became a success, Luck visited "Victoria" in Christchurch and was happy to find that she not only loved the song but had also split up with her abusive boyfriend.

524.content:
== Music video ==
A video was funded by the New Zealand Broadcasting Association but, unusually for the time, included a story rather than just a studio performance.

525.content: Shot in the band's hometown of Christchurch, it shows Luck as "Victoria"'s taxi driver and Al Park, a singer-songwriter sometimes credited as the father figure for the "Lyttelton Sound" and the first person to bring punk music to Christchurch.

526.content: In 2019, Luck covered Park's "I Walked Away" for the covers collection Better Already - The Songs Of Al Park.

527.content:
== Alternative versions ==
The recording of "Victoria" on the Prayers Be Answered album differs from the original single.

528.content: Another version was also included on the 1992 CD release of the 1986 Amplifier album.

550.content: Winter's Tale is a 1983 magic realism novel by Mark Helprin.

551.content: It takes place in a mythic New York City, markedly different from reality, and in an industrial Edwardian era near the turn of the 20th century.

552.content: Akiva Goldsman wrote a screenplay based on the novel and directed a feature film from the script, which was released in 2014.

553.content:
== Plot ==
An immigrant couple who were denied admission at Ellis Island due to consumption are forced to return to the ship which had brought them.

554.content: They break the display case containing a model of their ocean-going vessel and set their son Peter adrift in New York Harbor inside it.

555.content: He is found in the reeds and adopted by the Baymen of the Bayonne Marsh, who send him off to Manhattan when he comes of age.

556.content: There he first becomes a mechanic and then is forced to become a burglar in a gang called the Short Tails.

557.content: He soon makes a mortal enemy of their leader, Pearly Soames, and is constantly on the run from the gang.

558.content: Early one winter morning, Peter is on the brink of being captured and killed by the gang when he is rescued by a mysterious white horse called Athansor, who becomes his guardian.

559.content: While attempting to rob a house, Peter meets and falls in love with Beverly Penn.

560.content: The daughter of millionaire Isaac Penn, owner and publisher of the New York Sun, Beverly is eccentric, free-spirited, and enigmatic.

561.content: This captivates Peter initially, but her deeper nature is revealed with her terminal consumption.

562.content: Beverly never disappears from Peter's life, protecting him until the end.

563.content: His love for the dying Beverly causes him to become obsessed with justice.

564.content:
== Literary significance and reception ==
Winter's Tale was published in 1983.

565.content:
It was praised on the front cover of the New York Times Book Review (NYTBR) as "funny, thoughtful, passionate...large-souled."
People Magazine called it, "Entrancing, eccentric, hilarious, pierced by fantasy the way a storm is pierced by lightning."  Joyce Carol Oates called it, "A dazzling modern fairy tale by a storyteller of seemingly effortless and artless grace."  The reviewer for the New York Daily News said, "I have fallen in love with a book....The object of my affection is Mark Helprin's Winter's Tale....This sort of thing happens every now and then, usually about once a decade, and always, it seems, by surprise.

566.content:
The shock is all the greater when I find myself staying up, square-eyed from too much reading, until four in the morning, desperate to get to the end, at the same time hoping it never ends."
David Pringle, in the book Modern Fantasy: The 100 Best Novels, praised Winter's Tale as "a haunting piece of North American magic realism".

567.content: In May 2006, the New York Times Book Review published a list of American novels, compiled from the responses to "a short letter [from the review] to a couple of hundred prominent writers, critics, editors and other literary sages, asking them to identify 'the single best work of American fiction published in the last 25 years.'" Among the 22 books to have received multiple votes was Helprin's Winter's Tale.

568.content:
== Film adaptation ==
The film adaptation was released on Valentine's Day, 2014, written and directed by Akiva Goldsman as his directorial debut.

569.content: It starred Colin Farrell as Peter Lake, Russell Crowe as Pearly Soames, Jessica Brown Findlay as Beverly Penn, Jennifer Connelly as Virginia Gamely, and Will Smith as Lucifer though originally credited as "Judge".
